hook: A college says weekly nudge emails help students finish online courses, and its study gives a 95% interval for the difference in finishing rates from 0.03 to 0.11. Another study of snack sales at two stores gives an interval from $-0.04$ to 0.06. One interval supports a claim and the other does not. The difference is where 0 sits.

prereq.q: A 95% interval for $p$ is from 0.44 to 0.52. Is 0.5 a plausible value of $p$?
options: Yes, it is inside the interval
No, it is above the center
No, the interval is too wide
prereq.why: Values inside the interval are plausible.

prereq.q: What does the interval $(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \text{SE}$ estimate?
prereq.why: An interval estimates a parameter: the true difference.

figure.caption: Three 95% intervals for $p_1 - p_2$. Where 0 falls decides the claim each one supports.

chain.effect: ask whether 0 is a plausible value of $p_1 - p_2$, that is, whether it is inside the interval

chain.cause: Every value in the interval is greater than 0
chain.effect: the interval gives convincing evidence that $p_1 > p_2$ (less than 0: that $p_1 < p_2$)
equal proportions are plausible, so there is not convincing evidence of a difference, and the interval does not prove there is none

chain.cause: A claim names a value such as "15 points more"
chain.effect: check that value the same way: inside the interval means plausible, outside means convincing evidence against it

ideas: Entirely above 0: convincing evidence $p_1 > p_2$. Entirely below 0: convincing evidence $p_1 < p_2$. Contains 0: no convincing evidence of a difference.
Write the claim with the reason first: "Because every value in the interval is greater than 0, the interval gives convincing evidence that ..."
A 95% interval and a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ nearly always agree about whether 0 is plausible.
Containing 0 never proves the proportions are equal; very large samples can make even tiny differences convincing.

misconception.wrong: If the interval contains 0, the study proved that the two proportions are the same.
misconception.right: Containing 0 only means a difference of 0 is plausible. Other values in the interval are plausible too, so the right wording is "not convincing evidence of a difference".

summary: To judge a claim with an interval for $p_1 - p_2$, look at where 0, or the claimed value, sits. Entirely above or below 0 gives convincing evidence of a difference in that direction; an interval that contains 0 gives no convincing evidence of a difference, which is not proof of equality. State the reason, the evidence and the parameter in context.
